items.title: Supreme Court shifting to ecocentric approach; no automatic precedence for human interests: Justice BV Nagarathna
items.summary: The Supreme Court is pushing for a shift from an anthropocentric to an ecocentric approach in environmental cases, Justice BV Nagarathna recently said. Under ecocentric approach, human interests would not automatically take precedence over those of the non-human world, she explained. “This entails recognising that human interests do not, by virtue of being human, enjoy automatic precedence over the interests of the non-human world; rather, we bear obligations towards non-human life that exist independently of their utility to us,” she said. The judge was speaking at the valedictory session of the National Green Tribunal’s International Conference on “The Future of Environment and Climate Dynamics”. Justice Nagarathna said environmental adjudication require courts to look beyond completed violations and deal with risks that were unfolding in real time, often amid scientific uncertainty and with potentially irreversible consequences. “In that sense, environmental adjudication is an exercise in foresight, requiring courts to govern the present with an alert consciousness of the future,” she said. The Court took note of Banerjee's allegations of delay in adjudication of the dispute by ECI and asked for a reasonable time for final decision in the matter. "For how much time do you expect? Give us a reasonable timeframe in which the parties are given a fair opportunity to lead their evidence, but the matter is not prolonged and you also get sufficient time to apply your mind. Something realistic," CJI Kant asked the ECI. The matter will be heard next on September 28. Justice Joymalya Bagchi, CJI Surya Kant and Justice V Mohana The dispute arose after rival factions led by Mamata Banerjee and West Bengal Leader of Opposition Ritabrata Banerjee staked claim to the Trinamool Congress name, symbol and organisational control.

items.title: Stamping hurdle in enforcement of  arbitral awards
items.summary: Arbitration proceedings ought to resemble a 400-metre race - quick, direct and unhindered. In India, however, they have turned into something closer to a steeplechase, littered with hurdles. The recent judgment of the Delhi High Court in URC Construction (P) Ltd v. Airports Authority of India , pronounced on September 1, 2026, on the stamping of an arbitral award for enforcement proceedings under Section 36 of the Arbitration and Conciliation (A&C) Act, 1996, adds one more such hurdle. The tension between the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 and the A&C Act is not new. Whether a court can appoint an arbitrator under Section 11 of the A&C Act where the agreement is unstamped was hotly debated earlier. In NN Global v. Indo Unique Flame , a Constitution Bench, by a 3:2 majority, held that in case of an unstamped agreement, a High Court can proceed further under Section 11 of the A&C Act only once a certificate has been issued under Section 42(2) of the Stamp Act. In an earlier critique , I had observed that our approach remains rooted centuries back despite technological advancement and developments in arbitration law. items.title: Supreme Court refuses to halt forensic audit of Fortis transactions in Daiichi-Singh brothers dispute
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Friday refused to interfere with a Delhi High Court order directing a forensic audit of Fortis Healthcare in connection with the Daiichi Sankyo-Singh brothers dispute [ Fortis Vs Daiichi Sankyo]. However, a Bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana clarified that the High Court's observations against Fortis were only tentative and prima facie and would not bind the forensic auditor. The forensic audit will have to be conducted independently without being influenced by those observations. “It goes without saying that the forensic audit shall be conducted independently without being influenced by those observations made by the High Court, ” the Court added. The proceedings arose out of Daiichi Sankyo's efforts to enforce a 2016 arbitral award against the Singh brothers and other judgment debtors. The dispute subsequently expanded to examine what happened to the Singh brothers' substantial shareholding in Fortis while proceedings were pending before courts.
